title: Ramsar Convention and India's Ramsar Sites

cards.b:
Ramsar questions appear almost every year: which site is in which state, which sites are on the Montreux Record, what the criteria are, and how many sites India has. Site counts keep rising, so exams also test the latest additions.

This lesson holds the stable facts first and the changing numbers clearly marked "as of".

The Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat was signed at Ramsar, Iran, on 2 February 1971 and came into force in 1975. World Wetlands Day is observed on 2 February. The Secretariat is at Gland, Switzerland. India became a party on 1 February 1982.

It is the oldest modern global environmental treaty on one ecosystem. Its three pillars are wise use of all wetlands, designating Ramsar sites, and international cooperation. A listing does not take land from national control, and the site stays under national law.

A wetland qualifies if it meets at least one of nine criteria.

  • Criterion 1: a representative, rare or unique wetland type.
  • Criteria 2 to 6: biodiversity of species and communities. Criterion 5 is 20,000 or more waterbirds. Criterion 6 is 1 percent of a waterbird population.
  • Criteria 7 and 8: fish.
  • Criterion 9: 1 percent of a non-bird wetland-dependent animal population.

The definition of wetland is broad. It includes marshes, lakes, rivers, peatlands, mangroves, coral reefs, paddy fields, and marine water up to six metres deep at low tide.

The Montreux Record is a list of Ramsar sites where changes in ecological character have happened, are happening or are likely. It was set up in 1990 at a conference in Montreux, Switzerland. A listing is meant to draw help, not to punish.

India has two sites on the record: Keoladeo National Park (Rajasthan) and Loktak Lake (Manipur). Chilika (Odisha) was put on it and then removed in 2002, after restoration work and opening a new mouth to the sea. It was the first Asian site removed, and later won a Ramsar award.

cards.h: How the number grew (as of dates)
cards.b:
India's first two sites, Chilika and Keoladeo, were listed in 1981-82. The count was about 26 in 2014. It rose sharply in recent years:

  • about 49 as of August 2022
  • about 75 as of February 2023
  • about 85 as of August 2024
  • about 89 to 91 as of 2025

Counts change, so check the latest list. India has the largest Ramsar network in South Asia. Tamil Nadu has the most sites of any state, and Uttar Pradesh is next. The Sundarbans (West Bengal, 2019) is the largest Indian Ramsar site by area.

• Rajasthan: Keoladeo (Bharatpur), Sambhar Lake (salt lake).
  • Odisha: Chilika (largest coastal lagoon, brackish), Bhitarkanika mangroves.
  • Manipur: Loktak (floating phumdis, Keibul Lamjao, sangai deer).
  • Punjab: Harike, Kanjli, Ropar.
  • Kerala: Ashtamudi, Vembanad-Kol, Sasthamkotta.
  • Andhra Pradesh: Kolleru. Gujarat: Nalsarovar.
  • Ladakh: Tso Moriri. J&K: Wular, Hokersar.
  • Assam: Deepor Beel. Maharashtra: Lonar Lake (2020), Nandur Madhameshwar.
  • Madhya Pradesh: Bhoj Wetland, Sakhya Sagar.

India has no wetland-specific Act. The Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 replaced the 2010 rules under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986. They give State Wetlands Authorities the task of listing and regulating wetlands and set up a National Wetlands Committee. They ban conversion for non-wetland use, solid waste dumping and industry in notified wetlands. They exclude river channels, paddy fields and areas under the CRZ rules.

Schemes: the National Wetland Conservation Programme (1985-86), later merged into the National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems (NPCA, 2013). Amrit Dharohar (announced in the Union Budget 2023-24 and launched in June 2023) aims at the wise use of wetlands, local livelihoods, ecotourism and carbon stock.

A Ramsar tag brings attention and tourists, but it does not give legal protection by itself. Many sites sit inside national parks, like Keoladeo, and are protected by other laws. Others, like urban lakes and river stretches, have weak management.

Critics say states race to add sites for numbers. Supporters say listing brings management plans, funds and community involvement.

Keoladeo suffers from lack of water from the Gambhir river and invasive grass. Loktak's water level is changed by the Ithai barrage, which flooded phumdis and hurt fish. Harike is hit by water hyacinth and pollution. Wular and Dal face silt and encroachment. Wetlands also store flood water, recharge aquifers and hold carbon.

India's wetlands cover about 4.6 percent of land (Space Applications Centre atlas, 2011).

Prelims-style: "Which Indian sites are on the Montreux Record?" (Keoladeo, Loktak). "Ramsar sites are designated under which criteria?" (nine). "Which is the largest brackish water lagoon in India?" (Chilika).

Mains-style: "Why are wetlands called kidneys of the landscape? Discuss India's steps for their conservation." Structure: functions; Ramsar and numbers (as of year); Wetland Rules 2017; Amrit Dharohar; threats; community role; way forward.
